title: The Matewan Massacre
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Speaker 2, the show's co-host) cover the Matewan Massacre of May 1920 in Mate Wan (Matewan), a small town in Mingo County, southern West Virginia. They trace the background of coal company control, private police forces like the Baldwin-Felts Detective Agency, and the UMWA's organizing push. They describe the shootout in Matewan that killed Mayor Cabell Testerman and Albert Felts, the later assassination of Sid Hatfield and Ed Chambers at the McDowell County courthouse, the Battle of Blair Mountain, and the long-term effect on labor unions and the New Deal. The episode closes with a listener correction about Catalina Island and a brief reference to the 1987 John Sayles film Matewan.

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce live show dates in Seattle, Portland and Sketch Fest in San Francisco in January.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Mexico City travel and Speaker 2's enthusiasm for the city, then how the topic came up via Will Oldham and the John Sayles film Matewan.

segments.title: Pronouncing Matewan
segments.summary: Josh gives a mnemonic for pronouncing Matewan and the hosts joke about it.

segments.title: Introduction to the Matewan events
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Battle of Matewan as part of a series of incidents in southern West Virginia and Appalachia in the early twentieth century, with coal and labor history as the context.

segments.title: Coal, industrialization and company control
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how coal fueled American industrialization and how coal companies dominated mining towns, owning housing, businesses and even local law offices.

segments.title: Private police and divide-and-conquer tactics
segments.summary: Josh describes private police forces hired by operators and mine owner Justice Collins's strategy of mixing ethnic groups and paying them unequally to prevent unionizing.

segments.title: Integrated unionism and the UMWA founding
segments.summary: The hosts note that the union brought together diverse workers, including a cafeteria standoff at gunpoint, and that the United Mine Workers of America was founded in 1890.
topics: United Mine Workers of America founding

segments.title: Violence of early labor strikes
segments.summary: Josh describes how strikes were bloody, with people shot by both company and government forces, and notes the UMWA's 1897 strike and its later push into southern West Virginia.

segments.title: Paint Creek and Cabin Creek strike
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1912 Paint Creek and Cabin Creek strike in Kanawha County, the Baldwin-Felts guards, martial law under Governor Glasscock, and the arrest of union leaders including Mother Jones. They also outline the recurring pattern of evictions, tent cities, and attacks.

segments.title: Baldwin-Felts Detective Agency background
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Baldwin-Felts was founded in Roanoke in 1892 by William G. Baldwin and Thomas Felts, modeled on Pinkerton, and used for violent work including union busting.

segments.title: Colorado Ludlow massacre and tent city burnings
segments.summary: The hosts recount how Baldwin-Felts guards were involved in the 1914 Ludlow massacre in Colorado, where a tent city was burned and children died, and how such violence was common until the 1930s.

segments.title: Rising tensions and UMWA campaign in West Virginia
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1919 nationwide coal strike and a 1920 UMWA organizing campaign in southern West Virginia, with Mingo County at its center.

segments.title: Matewan town and Sid Hatfield
segments.summary: The hosts describe Matewan as an independent town not controlled by the mining company, with police chief Sid Hatfield, a pro-union lawman and a descendant of the Hatfield family.

segments.title: Stone Mountain Coal Company and spy C. Everett Lively
segments.summary: The hosts name the Stone Mountain Coal Company and describe spy C. Everett Lively, who ran a cafe that hosted union meetings while reporting to Baldwin-Felts. They also discuss union leader Frank Keeney and the secrecy around local leadership. Chuck mentions being born in Stone Mountain, Georgia.

segments.title: Events leading to the Matewan shootout
segments.summary: The hosts describe the May 19, 1920 Baldwin-Felts raid in Matewan to evict tent city families, with the Felts brothers and Cebe Cunningham involved, and the arrest attempt on Sid Hatfield.

segments.title: The Matewan shootout
segments.summary: The hosts recount the street gunfight in Matewan between Baldwin-Felts detectives and townspeople, with accounts differing on who fired first. Seven detectives were killed, including Albert Felts, along with Mayor Cabell Testerman and two miners. Some detectives fled across the river into Kentucky.

segments.title: Aftermath, rumors and Hatfield's marriage
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the bullet-marked brick buildings on Mate Street, a rumor that Hatfield shot the mayor over his wife Jesse, and Hatfield's trial and acquittal. Jesse later married Sid Hatfield and was a descendant of Randolph McCoy. The couple was arrested for cohabitation in Huntington before a judge allowed the wedding.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Trials, assassination of Hatfield and Chambers
segments.summary: Hatfield, Chambers and seventeen miners were acquitted in Mingo County. Hatfield and Chambers were later gunned down in McDowell County by C. Everett Lively and others, and the assassins were acquitted on self-defense grounds. Jesse Hatfield later remarried in 2022.

segments.title: Governor Morgan and the marchers
segments.summary: The hosts describe Governor Ephraim Morgan ignoring miners' demands after the killings, his election through a split progressive vote, and the US Senate's view of West Virginia as an industrial autocracy.

segments.title: Battle of Blair Mountain
segments.summary: About ten thousand miners marched toward Logan County in August 1921, facing Sheriff Don Chafin and his deputies on Blair Mountain. The several days of fighting included aerial bombing and gas, until federal troops under President Warren Harding arrived and the miners surrendered. Union membership later fell from 500,000 to 100,000 by 1929.

segments.title: Legacy of the mine wars and the New Deal
segments.summary: The hosts argue the mine wars drew national attention, helped elect FDR and the New Deal, and improved labor conditions. They note the UMWA's role in forming the CIO and that Baldwin-Felts operated until both founders died in 1936. They recommend the 1987 John Sayles film Matewan and recap Lively's downfall.

segments.title: Lively's restaurant and Brunswick Stew
segments.summary: The hosts briefly note that Lively's restaurant was shut down for health code violations, joking about a foot in the Brunswick stew, and refer to a past episode.

segments.title: Listener correction on Catalina Island
segments.summary: A listener corrects Josh's depiction of Catalina Island harbor in the Natalie Wood episode, describing it as a boater's campground rather than a yacht party scene, and questions the cries-for-help account.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for listener mail and the iHeartRadio credit.
